topics.title: 课程作业
topics.summary: EPFL guidelines for using AI in studying advise students that they should not use AI during exams or assessments unless explicitly allowed, and tell students to check their course policy or ask their instructor. Assessment material that is not the student's personal and original contribution must be recognizable as such under LEX 1.3.3 Article 4; guidelines advise disclosing AI-tool use in a statement and checking the course policy or instructor for its formulation.

claims.text: EPFL's studying guide states that assessment material not constituting the student's personal and original contribution must be recognizable as such under LEX 1.3.3 Article 4. It says the use of AI tools should be disclosed in a statement and directs students to check their course's specific AI policy or ask the instructor how to formulate it.

evidence.quote: EPFL rules (Lex 1.3.3, Article 4) require that all assessment material that is not the student’s personal and original contribution must be recognizable as such. Therefore, the use of AI tools should be disclosed in a statement. Check your course’s specific AI policy or ask your instructor how to formulate this statement.
evidence.title: Guidelines for using (Gen)AI in studying – Teaching ‐ EPFL

claims.text: EPFL recommends that teachers make explicit to students what AI use is not legitimate in a course and what rules accompany AI tool use.

evidence.quote: Since there is no ‘one-size-fits-all’ rule regarding the use of AI in assessment, it is recommended that teachers make explicit to students what kind of use is not legitimate in their course, and what rules accompany the use of AI tools.
evidence.title: AI tools and Student Assessment

claims.text: EPFL guidance specifies that submitting AI-generated content as one's own work without proper attribution is considered AI plagiarism. Tools specifically aiming to detect AI-generated content are not admissible as stand-alone evidence of AI plagiarism due to a high risk of false positives. Under continuous assessment procedures, where unauthorized AI use or non-disclosure is suspected, the course teacher writes a report and submits it with evidence to the section director and Legal Service (Affaires juridiques) for formal evaluation, which constitutes a referral of suspected misconduct rather than an adjudication of cheating.

topics.title: 隐私与敏感数据
topics.summary: EPFL advises students not to input confidential, private, or personal information into public generative AI tools because data is shared with private companies and control is lost. In the captured EPFL teaching guide, enterprise licenses such as Microsoft 365 Copilot via an EPFL account are described as unsuitable for regulated data because the guide states that EPFL has not signed a data processing agreement guaranteeing protections aligned with institutional needs or Swiss personal-data legislation; the current central-IT contract or tenant DPA status was not independently established in this review.

topics.title: 研究与成果出版
topics.summary: EPFL Library guidance clarifies that LLMs cannot be listed as authors or co-authors under the Swiss Copyright Act (Art. 6) because they lack accountability. Under EPFL Library's agreement with Elsevier, CC-BY open access content may be used with any AI tool, whereas for licensed closed or CC-BY-NC-ND publications, use is permitted with closed non-learning AI tools or with open learning tools operating in a secure, user-controlled environment (on-premises or solely for authorized users); commercial use is prohibited and publications must not reproduce closed or CC-BY-NC-ND content.

claims.text: EPFL Library guidance on scientific information for manuscripts intended for publication states that Large Language Models cannot be listed as authors or co-authors because they lack the ability to be accountable for the content they generate, citing the Swiss Copyright Act (Chapter 2, Art. 6). claims.text: According to EPFL Library's description of its agreement with Elsevier, open access publications with a CC-BY license may be used with any available AI tool, including for tool development and training, with free sharing of results. For licensed closed publications or Open Access publications under a restrictive CC-BY-NC-ND license where Elsevier owns all or key rights, use is permitted with closed versions of AI tools that do not train the algorithm or learn from/incorporate inputs (e.g. non-learning ChatGPT Team, potentially subject to fees/restrictions), or with open versions of learning AI tools or institutional tool/platform development provided they operate in a secure, user-controlled environment (self-hosted on-premises or externally hosted solely for Participating Institutions or Authorized Users). AI-generated results or platforms may be published for research and teaching provided they do not contain or reproduce closed or CC-BY-NC-ND content (linking is permitted), while commercial use of such AI-generated content or platforms is prohibited.

claims.text: EPFL study management regulations provide two formal procedures to oppose a grade or notified failure: an internal request for reassessment at EPFL within 10 days, or an external appeal to the Commission de recours interne des EPF within 30 days. Both deadlines are calculated from reception, at the address given by the student, of the grade or notified failure (transcripts sent by post). If a mark is contested on the grounds of an error in correction or assessment, the responsible teacher is the only person authorized to modify the mark subject to justification to the program direction; if contested for a formal defect, Legal Affairs reviews whether a significant formal defect impacted the result to warrant exam cancellation and repetition. Procedural costs are charged ahead of the procedure and refunded only if the student's claim succeeds. These rules govern academic grade disputes; whether specific appeal pathways or different deadlines apply to AI disciplinary misconduct sanctions is not established on this page and remains an evidence gap.

evidence.quote: There are two ways of opposing a grade or notified failure: a procedure at EPFL, called request for reassessment, and a procedure outside of EPFL, through the Commission de recours interne des EPF, called appeal.
evidence.title: Reassessment Request and Appeal – Education ‐ EPFL

evidence.quote: The deadline to start these procedures is within 10 days for the request for reassessment and within 30 days for the appeal. Both deadlines are calculated from the reception, at the address given by the student, of the grade or notified failure (transcripts sent by post).
evidence.title: Reassessment Request and Appeal – Education ‐ EPFL
evidence.location: lines 61-61; Reassessment request and appeal / Deadlines

evidence.quote: If a mark is contested on the grounds of an error in correction or assessment, the teacher responsible will be asked to check the correction. He/she is the only person authorized to make any corrections. If he/she modifies the mark, he/she must justify the modification to the program’s direction, who will check whether the reason is justified. If the result is contested on the grounds of a formal defect, the matter is referred to Legal Affairs, who can only conclude that the examination should be cancelled if the formal defect is significant and has been shown to have had an impact on the result.
evidence.title: Reassessment Request and Appeal – Education ‐ EPFL
